content: Many medications, including chloroquine, can affect heart rhythm by causing QT prolongation. Additionally, certain vaccines, such as the rabies and cholera vaccines, may be less effective if administered while you are taking chloroquine. In the event of an overdose, if the individual experiences severe symptoms like loss of consciousness or difficulty breathing, call 911 immediately. For less severe cases, contact a poison control center right away. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222, while Canadian residents can call 1-844-764-7669. If you are taking chloroquine for an extended period, regular medical and laboratory tests are recommended. These may include eye exams, reflex tests, liver and kidney function tests, EKGs, and complete blood counts. It is important to attend all scheduled medical and laboratory appointments. Stay indoors or in screened areas whenever possible. If you are using chloroquine to prevent or treat malaria, it should only be used for your current travel or condition. If you miss a dose of chloroquine, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is close to the time of your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular dosing schedule. Do not double the dose to catch up. Store chloroquine at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Avoid storing it in the bathroom. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. This medication may cause side effects such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, headache, and diarrhea. It can also lead to low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), with symptoms such as sudden sweating, shaking, hunger, blurred vision, dizziness, or tingling in the hands or feet. If you have diabetes, monitor your blood sugar levels regularly and report any symptoms of hypoglycemia to your doctor immediately. Chloroquine may cause serious eye or vision problems, especially with long-term use or high doses. This medication may lead to QT prolongation, a condition that affects heart rhythm. The risk of QT prolongation is higher if you have certain medical conditions, low potassium or magnesium levels, or are taking other medications that can cause QT prolongation. Conditions such as severe sweating, diarrhea, or vomiting, as well as the use of diuretics (water pills), may increase this risk. During pregnancy, chloroquine should only be used when clearly necessary, as it passes into breast milk. Always consult your doctor about the risks and benefits of using this medication during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Drug interactions may alter how your medications work or increase the risk of serious side effects. Keep a list of all the products you use, including prescription and non-prescription drugs and herbal products, and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. Many drugs besides chloroquine can affect heart rhythm (QT prolongation). This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about this product. It does not guarantee that the product is safe, effective, or appropriate for you. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information about this product and your specific health needs.
